Google has shipped four Gemini models in about five weeks, each named after an element on the periodic table, and the names won’t tell you which one to use. (Senior editor Jack Cheng https://every.?ev_audience=free and head of evals Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free each have a theory about the order.)

Gemini 4 Neon is the newest. Google pitches it as its midweight model: faster than Carbon https://every.?ev_audience=free and built to compete with Claude Opus and GPT-6.2 Sol. Three of us have tested it since the day it was announced, across coding, writing, and knowledge work, some of it live on Wednesday’s livestream.

What we found depends on whether you want a collaborator or a workhorse. With a person steering, Neon shows more taste than any Gemini model we’ve tested. Left alone on a long, detail-heavy job, it’s a different story.

Our Mini-Vibe Check gets into:

 * The slide deck Mike calls the best he’s seen from a Gemini model, and where Claude still beat it
 * Why Kieran Klaassen https://every.?ev_audience=free, creator of Compound Engineering, puts Neon alongside Opus for coding, and the one setting he says you can’t skip
 * The manifesto staff writer Katie Parrott https://every.?ev_audience=free stayed up until midnight writing with Neon, plus the AI habits she still had to edit out
 * What Neon found in our reader surveys that Mike never asked it to look for

There’s also a catch in the token bill, and it matters most if you’re paying by the token instead of through a Google subscription.

If you’re choosing between Hydrogen, Neon, and Carbon, the full review will help you decide which one fits your work. It’s for paid subscribers. Upgrade to read it, along with every Vibe Check we publish.
